genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a food depot
winter deliveries were arriving incomplete
the shops she supplied were running short of goods
she first blamed the hauliers and the suppliers
she understood that the muddle came from her own building
heavy goods were moved closer to the doors
lanes painted on the floor now organise movement
the handlers laughed at the change at first
the walking done by the teams grew shorter
not one order was missed the following season
text: The woman who runs a food depot knows the smell of damp cardboard better than anyone alive. Winter after winter the same ordeal came round: the lorries pulled in half empty, and the shops she was meant to supply ran short faster than she could fill them. She blamed the hauliers first, then the suppliers, before admitting that the muddle began inside her own building. So she thought the whole place through again. Heavy goods went by the doors, rare items to the back, and she painted coloured lanes across the floor that nobody crossed without a reason. The handlers laughed at her to begin with, then found their gain in it: their walking grew shorter. The season that followed, not one order was missed. She talks about it without pride, as a plain thing that took her several winters to notice.

units: two assembly workshops are set against each other
the first invested in a single costly machine
that machine cuts and folds with no operator
the second workshop lines up three modest benches set by hand
the output of the integrated plant beats that of the three benches
the single machine takes many seasons to pay for itself
a breakdown of the single machine halts all production
the modest benches are mended with ordinary parts
the integrated formula turns a profit if demand is steady and heavy
the writer concludes that the choice depends on the buyers
text: Setting the two assembly workshops side by side comes down to comparing two ways of committing money. The first backed a single costly machine, able to cut and fold with nobody at the controls. The second chose three modest benches, set by hand, which one operator watches in turn. On paper the integrated plant wins: it turns out more than its rival, and the line hand merely approves the settings. Watching them work softens that verdict. The single machine takes seasons to pay for itself, and the slightest breakdown freezes everything. The three benches seldom fail together, and they are mended offhand with ordinary parts. The integrated workshop turns a profit as soon as demand holds steady and heavy; the split workshop takes fitful orders better. The choice hangs on who is buying, not on the specification sheet.

units: the writer answers a request for advice in writing
the reader is starting out in the same trade
he advises reading contracts as far as the termination clauses
a shaky engagement shows itself in its annexes
he advises checking that the employer really pays the contributions
he advises keeping your payslips
he warns against rushing the pay talk out of embarrassment
a sum badly settled at the outset weighs for a long time
he urges keeping company with people in the same trade to hear about bad employers
the writer declares himself available should trouble arise
text: Madam, you asked what I would say to a beginner entering our trade, and I answer in writing gladly, so that nothing of it should get lost. First, contracts. Read them right through, the termination clauses included, for a shaky engagement gives itself away in its annexes rather than in its title. Second, cover. Make certain your employer truly pays the contributions owed for you, ask for your payslips and put them away. Third, pay. Do not rush a talk about money out of embarrassment: a sum badly settled at the outset will follow you through whole seasons. Fourth, company. Keep close to those doing the same work, for they will point you away from the doubtful houses. Lastly, spare your strength. I wish you a calm beginning, and I remain at your disposal should any trouble arise.

units: an employment adviser answers a run of questions
she puts the starting point in taking stock of your own skills
the second stage is spotting the employers who recruit without announcing it
then comes sending applications shaped to each firm
she warns that many refusals are to be expected
discouragement often arrives before the first interview
she advises writing every step down in a notebook
keeping that notebook turns waiting into actions you can measure
she advises preparing the interview by studying what the firm does
she urges against mistaking a slow selection for an injustice
text: Where does a job search begin? The adviser we questioned pushes the expected answer aside: you do not begin by writing, you begin by taking stock of what you can really do. And next? Next comes the stage of learning to prospect, that is, to spot the employers who are recruiting without saying so yet. Then you apply, one letter after another, shaping each one to the firm it goes to. How many refusals lie ahead? More than anyone pictures, she admits, and the weariness usually turns up before the first interview. What can be done then? Keep a notebook of every step taken, so that waiting becomes a run of actions you can measure. And the interview itself? You prepare it by studying what the firm does, instead of reciting your own path. Her last word is short: a slow selection is not an unjust one.

units: a neighbour tells the narrator about his picking season
he had been taken on for the length of the harvest
his pay depended on the number of crates filled
the crop came in heavy across the whole region
the buyers imposed half the usual price
the growers sold cheap to keep the fruit from rotting
the rate per crate came down
the pickers earned less for gathering more
he means to come back next season
he will insist on a rate written down before he leaves
text: Back from his picking season, the neighbour downstairs did not mince his words about any of it. He had been taken on for the whole harvest and paid by the crate, in an orchard where you slogged from first light to last. The crop had come in heavy everywhere, he told me, so the buyers laid down the law: they offered half the usual price, and the growers had to let their fruit go cheap rather than watch it rot. Down went the rate per crate, and the pickers earned less for gathering more. He shrugged his shoulders at me. When an orchard spills over, nobody gains, not even the one selling. He means to go back all the same, because he knows the place and knows where to sleep for nothing. But he warned me he would not set off again without a rate agreed beforehand and written on a signed paper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before common funds an accident ruined a family of craftsmen
the workshop hung on the bodily strength of one person
records tell of widows forced to sell the tools
apprentices were sent back to the countryside they came from
the answer came from the workshops themselves with no move from those in power
every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals
the fund replaced a ruined tool and kept an injured man fed
it also paid for the burial of a master craftsman
historians stress how slowly the idea took hold
the arrangement was later taken up by the public authorities
text: Before the trades gave themselves common funds, one accident was enough to ruin a family of craftsmen. The trouble was plain to all: the workshop rested on a single pair of hands, and those hands broke. Guild records describe widows forced to sell the tools in order to eat, and apprentices sent back to the countryside they had come from. The answer grew out of the workshops themselves, with no decree behind it. Every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals; the fund replaced a ruined tool, fed an injured man, met the burial costs of a master. What strikes historians is the slowness of the invention: it took generations to accept that a risk falls lighter when several carry it. Once the principle was granted, it ran from trade to trade, and the authorities copied it far later.

units: a fixed wage is likened to a river
the earnings of a self-employed worker are likened to showers
the wage earner can plan his spending because his income is regular
the self-employed worker knows rich spells and empty ones
the difference lies in regularity and not in the amount
on identical yearly earnings the self-employed worker gets a loan with more trouble
the lender is after regularity rather than wealth
the self-employed worker has to manufacture that regularity himself
he manages it by putting aside what the plentiful seasons leave him
text: A steady wage is much like a river, while the earnings of a self-employed worker are like rain. The river holds no more water than the rain does, but it flows. Whoever draws steady pay can plan his spending, sign a lease, promise a repayment, because he knows in advance the volume that will pass beneath his feet. Whoever lives on showers crosses rich weeks and dry ones: a great deal comes in, then nothing at all. The difference lies, then, not in the amount but in the shape of it. That is what lights up an odd fact: on equal yearly earnings, the second gets a loan with far more trouble than the first. A lender is not buying wealth, he is buying regularity. And the one who lives on rain must manufacture that regularity himself, by holding back what the plentiful seasons leave him.

units: a routine inspection was aimed at a packing plant
the inspector noted faults of four different kinds
pallets of resin were stored too close to the ovens
that exposure to heat explained the warping of certain batches
the dosing unit had gone too long without calibration
the setters corrected its drift by hand without writing it down
half the night shift lacked the certificate required
the pieces thrown out appeared in no accounting record
the site manager blamed the pressure of orders
the inspector puts these faults down to checking neglected over and over
text: It was meant to be a routine check at a packing plant, and the inspector came away from it with faults of four different kinds. Materials to begin with: the pallets of resin stored by the ovens had passed the heat tolerance, which explained the warped batches. Machines next: the dosing unit was running with no recent calibration, and its drift had been made good by hand by the setters, who had written none of it down anywhere. Staffing after that: half the night shift held posts without the certificate. Paperwork last: the pieces thrown out showed up nowhere at all in the production accounts. The manager of the site pleaded the pressure of the orders coming in. The inspector replied that nothing she had just found came from haste, but from checking done badly, season after season.

units: the procedure covers the opening of a retail shop
the steps must not be swapped around
the first is to gauge what the neighbourhood wants
that gauging goes through watching the passers-by and the shopfronts nearby
declaring the activity comes before any order of stock
the lease must carry a clause allowing you to leave
the first range is deliberately narrow to spare the cash
a trial week without advertising serves to adjust the prices
a record of goods in and goods out is kept from the first sale
text: Take these steps one by one in the order given, for the opening of a retail shop allows no swapping about. Start by gauging what the neighbourhood wants: count the passers-by, note the shopfronts nearby, ask those who live round about. Declare your activity next with the register kept for it, since no stock whatever may be ordered before that formality. Negotiate the lease then, insisting on a clause that lets you leave, for a badly chosen unit is harder to quit than to take. Build your first range after that, deliberately narrow: better to run short of an item than to lock up your cash. Open the doors quietly, without any fanfare, for a trial week, so as to adjust prices and hours. Keep, lastly, from the very first sale, a record of everything coming in and everything going out.

units: the closing of a cannery has been announced
the plant bought the catch of the fleet nearby
the skippers go out less and sell direct at a loss
the boatyards have cut their staff
the shops on the main street see fewer customers
the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally
elected members are calling for an investor to take the site over
no candidate has come forward because of the cost of renewing the cold chain
an association of employees proposes buying the plant together
the outgoing management has made no answer to that proposal
text: Since the closing of the cannery was announced, the employment area around it has taken one blow after another. The plant bought the catch of the local fleet; with no outlet left, the skippers put to sea less and sell direct, at a loss. The boatyards, which lived on their repair orders, have cut their staff in turn. The shops along the main street already report fewer customers, because the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally. Elected members are calling for an investor to take the site over, yet no candidate has come forward, the cold chain needing a costly renewal. An association of employees puts up another way out: buy the plant together and turn it to goods made in small runs. The outgoing management has made no answer. What becomes of the area will hang on that reply.
